newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Milosevic says OSCE can verify elections.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Milosevic says OSCE can verify elections.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic offered on Friday to let international observers check the fairness of elections which prompted Western condemnation after opposition parties claimed the vote was rigged.
Hours later, the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition and Belgrade students staged the biggest protests in Belgrade so far.
Milosevic, under severe U.S. pressure, protested in a letter to Secretary of State Warren Christopher that Serbia had a healthy democracy and accused Zajedno of "political terrorism".
Zajedno has waged more than three weeks of peaceful street protests since claiming it was cheated of victory during the November 17 local elections by Milosevic's ruling socialists.
More than 200,000 students and opposition supporters joined a 26th day of demonstrations in Belgrade, cramming the city centre and adjoining streets.
Belgrade students broke another record, staging a 20-km (12-mile) march across the city.

Milosevic proposed that the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) should check the November vote in which Zajedno said the socialists suffered their worst defeat in 50 years of unbroken rule.
Belgrade's state-controlled media carried the text of Milosevic's reply to demands from Christopher that the Serbian leader abide by the election result and promote democracy.
Milosevic said daily demonstrations calling for his overthrow had given the world a "distorted picture" of the conflict, and added:
"Democracy in Serbia has a long-standing tradition...I believe that our system is very good."
Zajedno accused the socialists of stuffing ballot boxes in provincial towns. In Belgrade, the socialists initially admitted defeat before accusing Zajedno of "irregularities" which the courts upheld.
The opposition was supported by the independent Humanitarian Law Centre which distributed a claim by jurists and members of Belgrade University law faculty that the election law was "defective".

They said courts, including the supreme court, had ignored evidence and failed to explain their reasons for refusing all 91 Zajedno appeals against disqualification. The only appeal upheld was made by the socialists.
Zajedno was angered by Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini who said in Belgrade on Thursday that it was unrealistic to expect reinstatement of the election result.

Although he spoke for himself and not for the United States or other Western governments, his remarks reinforced Zajedno's fear that a backroom deal was being worked out to give Milosevic an escape route.
Political sources said it was probably too late to reinstate the election result without the socialists admitting fraud, which the Serbian leader would not tolerate.
There was concern that the OSCE was being brought in to engineer a clean bill of health for Milosevic, who is regarded as a mainstay of Balkan security.
The OSCE said it had received no invitation from Milosevic. The organisation's standing in Yugoslavia is not high after the chaos surrounding elections that it supervised in Bosnia in September.
In an interview with the Rome daily La Repubblica on Friday Dini also ruled out Milosevic's resignation as a solution.
"No, absolutely (not). Milosevic does not intend to step down and I told the opposition clearly that this is not what the international community seeks," Dini said.
He urged "a political solution which allows for the establishment of solid rules for the future. Above all, for the elections to be held next year."
Serbia is due to hold presidential and parliamentary elections in 1997 which will require close international scrutiny to yield a credible result.
Before the municipal poll fiasco, socialist leaders boasted that the republican elections would cement Milosevic and his party securely in power for the next decade.
Opposition leaders claimed the local elections showed the reality of one-party rule in Serbia despite the appearances of multi-party democracy.
